sum: Durvāsā, a sage, offers Indra a garland. Indra, preoccupied, drapes it on his elephant Airāvata, who tosses it to the ground and tramples it. Durvāsā curses the gods to lose their prosperity.
why: Opens the mythic frame with a small act of carelessness that becomes a catastrophe; pride and its price.
turn: The elephant drops the garland and it is crushed.
story: Indra’s court at full radiance: gold, pearl, music, every colour at its brightest. Durvāsā enters, unhurried, with a garland he means as a gift. Indra, half listening, takes it without looking and drapes it over Airāvata’s head. The great white elephant shakes it off and the garland falls under his foot. The court goes quiet. Durvāsā looks at the crushed flowers, then at Indra, who has still not understood what he has done. The sage speaks one sentence, a curse, and walks out through the light. The shot ends on the flowers.

pl: Heaven; the field of battle; the gods’ flight
sum: Prosperity drains from heaven. Colour fades from armour and court; strength leaves the Devas. The Asuras overrun them and the Devas flee as suppliants.
why: Sets up the world in need: the powerful become petitioners, the cost of pride.
turn: Indra’s thunderbolt fails; the Devas run.
story: The curse takes hold. Colour leaves the banners first, then the armour, then the faces. The Devas’ strength drains with it; Indra’s thunderbolt flickers and goes out. The Asuras come in from the edges, brighter than the gods now. The gods run. Some stop to help the fallen; most do not. The last image is the court, grey, with the garland’s crushed flowers still on the floor, and a long line of gods walking out of it.

t: The petition to Brahmā and the Lord’s counsel
pl: Brahmā’s realm; the shore of the Ocean of Milk
sum: The Devas go to Brahmā, who takes them to Viṣṇu. A voice answers: make an alliance with your enemies and churn the Ocean of Milk for amṛta; the Lord will arrange the rest.
why: Delivers the plan and the film’s grammar lesson: the Lord acts through others and is never in the room.
turn: The voice says, in effect, “you will do it, and I will hold what you cannot.”
story: The Devas go to Brahmā, who takes them across the sky to the shore of the Ocean of Milk. The water is still and white. They kneel. Nothing appears. A light moves across the surface, a voice speaks, and Brahmā alone hears it clearly. He turns to Indra and passes it on: make peace with your enemies, churn this ocean for nectar, and the rest will be held for you. The Devas look at one another. It is not what they wanted to hear. The camera stays on their faces.

sum: The Devas, proud and desperate, approach Bali and the Asuras and propose to churn the ocean together. Each side hides its own motive: the Devas want the nectar for themselves, the Asuras expect an equal share.
why: A pact of rivals that cannot hold; seeds the “seizing is not holding” theme.
turn: Indra bows to ask Bali for help.
story: Indra goes to Bali under a flag of truce. The two courts meet on neutral ground. Each side watches the other’s hands. Indra says the thing he did not want to say: they need each other. Bali listens. He knows exactly what the gods want and means to take his share anyway. A cup is passed. No one drinks. Both sides agree, each believing they have fooled the other.

t: The mountain sinks; Kūrma lifts it
pl: The shore and the Ocean of Milk
sum: Mandara is carried to the shore and used as the churning rod. It sinks. The two armies stare at the water. The mountain rises again, and the audience sees only a vast curved back beneath it: Kūrma, the tortoise.
why: The film’s clearest image of the unseen support: the Lord as landform under everything.
turn: Something rises under the mountain.
story: The mountain is brought to the shore and set upright in the ocean as the churning rod. It begins to sink. The two armies stare as it goes down under their rope. For a long moment there is only water. Then it rises, slowly, on something vast and curved beneath it. A shell-like back, ridged and wet, lifts the mountain clear. No one speaks. The armies pick up the rope.

sum: The Devas hold the tail and the Asuras the head of Vāsuki. They pull in turn; the mountain spins, the sea convulses, the serpent breathes fire and smoke. Hands blister, strength fails, and something unseen empowers both sides.
why: Endurance as action; the long middle of the myth; the shared labour whose prize will not be shared.
turn: The mountain keeps turning, as if lifted by a hand no one sees.
story: The Devas hold the tail, the Asuras the head. They pull in turn. The mountain spins on the Lord’s back and the ocean turns with it. The serpent coughs smoke. Hands blister, backs bend, teeth set. A rhythm builds: pull, release, pull. Every strain is visible and no one sees what keeps the mountain from falling. A drop of nectar-white foam rises, and then another, and the sea begins to cloud. Both sides are exhausted. Neither lets go.

pov: The shore-watcher (fisher family) and the Devas
sum: The churning brings up the poison Hālāhala. It spreads on the water like black smoke. Beings flee in panic; fish die; the fisher child on the shore backs away from the water. Brahmā and the Devas call to Śiva.
why: The cost of the prize arrives first: before the gift, the poison.
turn: A single fisher child stays at the water’s edge.
story: The churning brings something up that is not nectar. A black stain spreads over the milk-white water. It moves faster than a man can run. Fish turn white and float. The Devas and Asuras drop the rope and flee along the shore. At the edge of the water, a fisher child stays where she is, one hand held out toward the dark. Brahmā calls to Śiva. No one else moves toward it.

pl: The shore of the Ocean of Milk
sum: Śiva walks toward the poison, cups it in his hand and drinks. Pārvatī’s hand rises to his throat to hold it there, and his throat turns blue. The Devas and Asuras stand silent. The churning resumes.
why: The first great act of absorption: one person walks into the harm so everyone else can live. Mirrors later acts by Krishna and Rukmini.
turn: Pārvatī’s hand closes on his throat.
story: Śiva walks toward the poison while everyone else runs from it. He kneels, cups it in one hand and lifts it. He drinks. Pārvatī’s hand rises to his throat, and holds. The skin there turns blue. For a long moment nothing else moves. Then the water begins to clear, a little at a time. The fisher child sees it. Behind her, someone starts to pull the rope again.

sum: With the poison held, the treasures rise: Surabhi the cow, the horse Uccaiḥśravā, the elephant Airāvata, the Kaustubha jewel, the Pārijāta tree, the Apsarās. Each is claimed. The jewel goes to the Lord, though no one sees the hand.
why: A scene of wonder and greed; each claim shows who the claimant is. Plants the Pārijāta tree.
turn: The jewel is taken by an unseen hand and no one protests.
story: With the poison held, the sea gives gifts. A cow rises, then a white horse, then an elephant like Airāvata, then a jewel that catches the sun. A tree comes up with flowers already open. Apsarās step from the foam. The Devas and Asuras claim them. A hand at the edge of the frame takes the jewel and no one objects. Nobody remarks on whose hand it was.

sum: Lakṣmī emerges from the ocean with a garland. Gods, sages and Asuras stand ready, each certain she will choose them. She looks at each and passes on. At the end she walks to the one who has not stepped forward and places the garland on him; he holds her to his chest for good. The Asuras are left empty-handed.
why: The mythic mirror of Rukmini’s choice; the theme in one image: she chooses, she is not taken.
turn: She passes every claimant and goes to the one who did not ask.
story: Lakṣmī rises from the sea with a garland in her hands. The gods and the Asuras stand in a long arc, each sure it will be him. She walks along the line. She looks at each face for a moment and moves on. She passes the powerful and the proud and the handsome. At the end of the line she stops in front of the one who has not stepped forward, and she places the garland on him. The shot cuts so that we see only the garland settle on a shoulder. Behind her, the line goes quiet.

sum: The Asuras stand where Lakṣmī passed them. Bali and his captains feel the refusal. Vāruṇī, the wine goddess, rises from the sea and Viṣṇu gives her to the Asuras as a consolation. They accept her.
why: Shows the rejected side as human; sets up the rage that will break the alliance.
turn: They take Vāruṇī and swallow their anger.
story: The Asuras stand where Lakṣmī passed them. Bali and his captains keep their faces still. The line shifts, and someone laughs. The wine goddess rises from the sea, and the Lord’s permission comes from offstage. The Asuras accept her. They take the cup and swallow their anger. They know exactly what they have lost.

t: Dhanvantari and the seizure of the pot
sum: Dhanvantari rises from the ocean carrying the pot of amṛta. The Asuras seize it in a rush. They begin to fight each other over who drinks first.
why: Greed turns winners against each other the moment they hold the prize: “seizing is not holding”.
turn: The pot passes between hands and the circle breaks.
story: Dhanvantari rises from the water holding a pot, and the Asuras go for it before he can say a word. Hands close on the handles. The pot passes from one to the next. Someone shouts that he saw it first. Someone else answers with a blow. The circle that held for the whole churning breaks. The gods watch from the edge, unmoving.

sum: A beautiful woman appears. The Asuras, captivated, ask her to distribute the nectar. She separates the two sides and serves the Devas first. The Asuras realise too late.
why: A deception sequence closer to a heist; moral grey: the right side is served by a trick.
turn: The ladle goes to the Devas’ side.
story: A woman walks into the assembly and the Asuras forget what they were arguing about. They ask her to share the nectar fairly. She smiles, separates the two sides into two lines, and begins to serve. The first ladle goes to the Devas. Then the second. The Asuras are still looking at her face when they realise the pot is nearly empty.

sum: Rāhu disguises himself as a Deva and sits in the line to drink. The sun and moon recognise him and cry out. The Sudarśana disc flashes; his head is cut off but survives, because the nectar has touched it.
why: A traitor, a refusal to be shut out, and a head that survives. A short sharp reversal.
turn: Sūrya and Candra point.
story: In the line of Devas, one face is not quite right. The sun and the moon see it first. They point and cry out. A flash of light crosses the line. The false god’s head leaves his body, and the head does not die. It rolls, blinks, and keeps looking at them. Behind it the body falls. The nectar has already reached the throat.

pl: The battlefield between heaven and ocean
sum: The alliance collapses; the Asuras attack. Bali leads them with illusions; Indra leads the Devas with the thunderbolt. Weapons and magic fill the field. The Devas turn the war and regain heaven.
why: The cosmic action set-piece; shows the cost of a pact of rivals; gives heaven back.
turn: The thunderbolt turns the field.
story: The alliance ends. The Asuras strike first with illusions: fire that is not fire, armies that vanish when struck. Bali leads from the front. Indra answers with the thunderbolt, and the field flashes. For a while the Devas lose ground. Then nectar-strength takes hold, and every blow they land is real. The line turns. Colour comes back across the field, banner by banner. The Devas return to heaven, which has its light again.

sum: Śiva, having heard of Mohinī, asks to see her. She appears in the forest; he is bewildered and pursues, then recognises the power behind the form and is released.
why: Even the wise are undone by wonder; recognition after bewilderment; an optional echo of the film’s reveal.
turn: He recognises the power behind the form.
story: Śiva has heard of the form that deceived the Asuras and asks to see it. Mohinī appears in a forest, in a light that seems to hold still for her. He looks, and the wisest of the gods stops thinking. He follows her between the trees. She runs, laughing, and he runs after. At the end of it he understands whose power this was. He stops, recognises it and is released. He stands still for a long moment, and then he laughs too.

t: The fisher family on the shore
pl: The shore of the Ocean of Milk
sum: A fisher family lives by the water. A child dips a hand into the sea and brings it up clean after the poison is held. Later a net comes up full of silver. The family does not know why; they live by the result.
why: World-welfare proof for Event 01; the person who benefits without knowing the cause.
turn: The child’s hand comes out clean.
story: On the shore a fisher family mends nets. The sea has been strange for days. A child kneels at the water’s edge and dips a hand in. She lifts it out and looks: it is clean. She holds it up to her mother. Later, at dusk, the net comes up full of fish that shine like silver. The family does not know why. They know that they are alive, and that the water is theirs again.

pl: Ambikā’s temple at Kuṇḍina; childhood or the eve of the wedding
sum: A girl, or Rukmini a few days before the wedding, studies a painted wall at the temple of Ambikā. Panels show the Churning: the mountain, the serpent, the poison, the goddess’s hand at Śiva’s throat, Lakṣmī choosing. A priest answers a question. Rukmini stops at the panel where Lakṣmī chooses.
why: Delivers the Manthana into Rukmini’s world and plants the temple where she will later pray.
turn: She stops at the panel of the choosing.
story: In the temple of Ambikā, Rukmini stops in front of a painted wall. A priest has been sweeping. The panels show a mountain, a serpent, a dark flood, a goddess’s hand at a god’s throat, and a goddess with a garland walking along a line of suitors. Rukmini asks who the goddess chose. The priest tells her. She stays at the last panel a long time, then touches the painted figure at the end of the line with one finger.

t: The bard’s recital on the eve of the wedding
sum: A bard, among the entertainers at the palace before the wedding, recites the Churning to a hall of kings who do not notice they are the Asuras. Rukmini, at the edge of the women’s gallery, hears the part about the goddess who passed every claimant.
why: Delivers the Manthana to the kings and Rukmini together; the audience sees the irony the kings do not.
turn: Rukmini realises the kings are the Asuras.
story: On the eve of the wedding, a bard sings in the hall. The kings are eating and drinking and half listening. He sings the Churning: the gods who lost their glory, the allies who were enemies, the poison, the goddess with the garland. He sings of the line of claimants and of the one she chose. The kings applaud, because they think it is about the gods. Rukmini, in the gallery above, watches them and sees the Asuras.

pl: Fields and roads across a kingdom
sum: Armies of arrogant kings tramp across fields and villages. Crops are crushed, wells fouled, animals taken. A cow stumbles under the weight of an army’s shadow and goes down on her knees.
why: Gives the film its first image of suffering and the reason the story needs a saviour.
turn: The cow falls.
story: Armies of arrogant kings cross a country. Chariots flatten the barley and the soldiers drag women’s grindstones along with them. Wells are fouled and granaries emptied, and village after village watches from its doorway. Somewhere under the weight of it all, a cow stumbles and goes down on her knees. The line of marching men does not break step. It goes around her.

sum: The Earth, in the form of a tearful cow, comes to Brahmā and tells him her suffering: too many arrogant kings, too much weight.
why: The plea that triggers the whole chain of events; a world crying for help.
turn: Brahmā rises to take her to the Lord.
story: The Earth comes to Brahmā as a cow, weeping. She cannot say it all at once. The kings are too many, too proud and too heavy. Brahmā puts a hand on her head. She looks up. He rises, and he does not need to be asked to lead the way.

pl: The shore of the Ocean of Milk
sum: Brahmā, Śiva and the Devas take the Earth to the shore of the same Ocean of Milk and worship Viṣṇu with the Puruṣa-sūkta hymn. The water is still. Brahmā goes into trance.
why: Rhymes with the Manthana; the shore is the film’s place of petitions.
turn: Brahmā’s trance begins.
story: Brahmā, Śiva, the Devas and the Earth come to the shore of the Ocean of Milk. The sea is flat, white and silent. They begin the hymn to the Lord. It rises, grows, and then fades to nothing. Brahmā’s eyes close. He does not move. The waters hold their breath.

sum: In trance Brahmā hears a voice from the sky. He relays it: the Lord already knows the Earth’s distress. The Devas are to take birth among the Yadus; he himself will come as Vasudeva’s son and lighten the Earth’s load by his own power of time.
why: The film’s promise: the answer arrives before the man. The cleanest example of the unseen-support grammar.
turn: Brahmā opens his eyes and repeats the voice.
story: In trance, Brahmā hears a voice from the sky. He opens his eyes slowly and speaks as if repeating something he has just learned by heart. The Lord already knows the Earth’s distress. The Devas are to take birth among the Yadus. He himself will appear as Vasudeva’s son, and lighten the Earth’s load through his own power of time. The Devas look up. There is nothing to see, and they bow anyway.

sum: Brahmā tells the Devas: be born among the Yadus; the Lord will be Vasudeva’s son; Ananta will come first as his elder brother; Yogamāyā will appear to carry out his work. The Devas’ wives will be born to be with him.
why: Lays the cast: Balarama (Ananta) and the hidden hand (Yogamāyā).
turn: Each Deva bows to take the assignment.
story: Brahmā tells the Devas how it will be. They will be born among the Yadus. Ananta will come first, as the elder brother. The Lord’s power of illusion will carry out his work. The Devas’ wives will be born to be with him. One by one, the Devas bow to take their assignment. The scene is quiet and almost administrative. It feels like a promise being filed.

sum: Brahmā returns to his abode. Śūrasena rules from Mathurā, which becomes the Yadu capital. The stage is set.
why: A bridge to Event 03; sets the city that will be besieged.
turn: A distant drum under the city’s quiet.
story: Brahmā goes home. In Mathurā, Śūrasena rules from a quiet court. The city goes about its day: carts, water, a bell. A drum sounds somewhere inside the quiet. The audience has just been told something is coming, and this is the place it will come to.

sum: A farmer and his cow plough a strip beside a road armies use. In one image the ground is trampled; in the last the cow lies down in the furrow and the plough turns clean soil.
why: World-welfare proof for Event 02; the burden lifted at ground level.
turn: The cow lies down in the furrow.
story: A farmer and his cow plough a strip beside the road that armies use. In the first shot the ground is trampled and the cow limps. Time passes. In the last, the cow lies down in the furrow, rests, and the plough turns clean soil. The farmer sits at the field’s edge and does not know why the road has gone quiet.

t: The cow that will not move
sum: An army passes through a street. A cow stops in the road and will not move. The soldiers curse her; an old woman says the story of the Earth who wept. Rukmini, on her way home, hears it and stops.
why: Delivers Event 02 into Rukmini’s world through an image she can see and a story she can hear.
turn: Rukmini stops walking and listens.
story: A column of soldiers comes through a street in Kuṇḍina. A cow stops in the middle of the road and will not move. The soldiers curse her and push. Rukmini, on her way home, slows. An old woman beside her says quietly, “She is the Earth, you know.” And she tells it: the weeping, the voice, the promise. Rukmini stands still long after the soldiers have gone around.

sum: Visitors sing Krishna’s praises in the palace and begin, not with his beauty, but with the reason: the Earth wept, a voice answered, a child was promised. Rukmini listens at the edge of the hall.
why: Turns the first “songs about him” from praise into a story with a cause; Event 02 lands in the first Krishna scene of the film.
turn: One visitor says the Earth wept for him.
story: Visitors sing in the palace. The first begins not with Krishna’s face but with the reason he came. The Earth wept, he says, and a voice answered. A child was promised. The next singer adds the cowherds, the third the beauty. Rukmini, at the edge of the hall, notices that all three start with the weeping. She decides to hear more.

sum: Asti and Prāpti, Kaṁsa’s widows, come home to their father Jarasandha and tell him how their husband died. His grief becomes rage and he resolves to destroy the Yādavas.
why: Gives the antagonist a human grievance; rage born of loss.
turn: He stands and calls for the army.
story: Two widows in white come into Jarasandha’s hall and stand before the throne. They do not weep. They say what happened to their husband Kaṁsa and who did it. The king sits very still. Then his hand closes on the arm of the throne, and he calls for the army. Courtiers move before he finishes the sentence.

sum: Twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs surround Mathurā. The water-carrier on the wall sees tents, banners and smoke to every horizon. The first chalk mark will be made on this day.
why: Scale and dread from the ordinary person’s eye; the siege as a visual fact.
turn: The army’s line closes to the horizon.
story: The army arrives in stages. First a line of dust, then tents, then banners, then a country of fires. The water-carrier on Mathurā’s wall puts down his bucket and counts, and gives up. By evening the horizon is full. He makes a first chalk mark on the wall, because there is nothing else to do.

sum: Krishna considers the situation. He will destroy the army but leave Jarasandha alive so that he gathers more armies, bringing more of the Earth’s burden into his hands. He says so, in effect, to Balarama; Balarama does not fully understand.
why: Mercy as strategy; the film’s clearest statement of Krishna’s method; links to Event 02.
turn: Balarama sits down, unconvinced but silent.
story: In a council room, Krishna’s voice lays out the plan: break the army, but leave the king alive. Jarasandha will raise another and another, and each will bring more of the Earth’s weight within reach. Balarama listens with a hard face. He does not see why a man who burns villages should be allowed to walk home. He sits down without agreeing. The scene ends on his silence.

sum: Two radiant chariots, with drivers and weapons, descend from the sky. Krishna and Balarama ride out with a small contingent. The conch sounds, and the enemy trembles before anything is seen.
why: Pure effect: the sound before the sight; the first spectacle of the unseen hero.
turn: The conch sounds and the front line steps back.
story: Two chariots drop from the sky in a column of light. They land on the plain outside Mathurā. Two men step up into them. The gate opens and a small column rides out. A conch sounds, long and clear, and the front line of Jarasandha’s army steps back before anything else has happened.

sum: Jarasandha mocks Krishna as a boy and challenges Balarama. A voice answers: heroes show their courage in action, not in boasting.
why: A portrait of Krishna through his enemy’s contempt; the rival’s disdain that the audience reads as respect.
turn: The reply is calm and shuts him up.
story: Jarasandha rides forward and calls across the field. He mocks the boy who hides behind a plough and offers Balarama a real fight. The answer comes back over the field in a quiet voice: heroes do not boast, they act. Jarasandha laughs, and the laugh stops short. Behind him, no one else is laughing.

t: The battle seen from the wall
pl: The walls of Mathurā; the plain
sum: The enemy surrounds the two chariots. The women on the wall watch and faint when the chariots vanish behind the enemy. Arrows destroy elephants, horses and chariots; the plough sweeps the infantry. The women wake to see the field empty of the enemy.
why: The battle as effect, not as spectacle of Krishna: the camera stays on the women.
turn: They wake to a cleared field.
story: The enemy closes on the two chariots. On the wall of Mathurā the women watch as the chariots disappear behind dust and men. One by one they faint. On the field, arrows fall on elephants and horses and chariots; the plough sweeps the footsoldiers aside. When the women wake the dust is thinning, and the plain is empty of the enemy. The chariots stand where they stood.

sum: Balarama seizes Jarasandha and begins to bind him. Krishna’s word stops him: not yet, there is a purpose. The king is released.
why: A small fight with a large moral turn; Balarama’s impatience set against Krishna’s purpose.
turn: Balarama’s hands open.
story: Balarama has Jarasandha by the throat and a rope in his other hand. He starts to bind him. A hand rises at the edge of the frame, and a word follows. Balarama stops. He looks at the rope, then at the hand, and opens his fist. Jarasandha stumbles back and runs. Balarama watches him go with something close to disgust.

pl: The road from Mathurā to Magadha
sum: Ashamed, Jarasandha resolves on penance. Other kings dissuade him: his defeat was fate, not failing. He turns back toward Magadha.
why: A chance at change refused; the coalition’s habit of consoling itself instead of learning.
turn: He allows himself to be talked out of it.
story: Jarasandha rides home alone with a few commanders. He stops by a river and says he will give it all up and do penance. The other kings who have come with him object. This was fate, they say, not failing. The river runs on. He looks at his hands, and then he gets back on the horse.

pl: The wall of Mathurā, across seasons
sum: A water-carrier chalks a mark on the wall after each siege. Each time the enemy comes in a new way: a night assault, a fire assault, an elephant charge, a flood. Each time it ends the same. The marks reach seventeen.
why: Tragic repetition turned into a single image; an enemy who cannot learn.
turn: The seventeenth mark is made, with no army to follow it.
story: The water-carrier’s wall in Mathurā. A night assault comes with torches, and is gone by morning. He makes a mark. A fire assault, with burning carts. A mark. An elephant charge. A mark. Siege towers. A mark. A flood. A mark. Each time it ends the same way, and each time the king is let go. The wall grows seventeen strokes long. On the last the carrier steps back, and there is no army to follow it.

sum: Krishna returns amid celebration and flowers. He gives the battlefield wealth to Ugrasena, the king, and takes none himself.
why: Shows his lack of acquisitiveness and the city’s relief.
turn: The king receives the wealth.
story: Krishna’s chariot comes back through the gate and the city throws flowers. Ugrasena waits in the courtyard. A hand holds out the wealth of the field and the king receives it. Nothing else is taken. The crowd cheers, and a child runs to the wheels of the chariot and has to be pulled back. The hand has already gone.

pl: The road from Mathurā to the hills
sum: After the cave, Jarasandha returns with twenty-three divisions while the Yadavas carry wealth toward Dvārakā. Krishna and Balarama run on foot. Jarasandha pursues, laughing.
why: The last chase; the brothers as fugitives; tonal reversal.
turn: They leave the road and climb.
story: Jarasandha returns with twenty-three divisions while the Yādavas carry wealth toward the sea. Two men leave the road and run. Behind them the king rides, laughing, with a host filling the road. The two men get smaller and the host does not. They turn off the plain and begin to climb.

sum: The brothers climb Pravarṣaṇa. Jarasandha cannot find them and sets the hill on fire. Two brothers on a mountain on fire, with no army: the only time they are afraid.
why: The two brothers’ lowest point; fear, not strategy.
turn: They run out of ground.
story: The hill is called Pravarṣaṇa. They go up it because there is no other way to go. The king below cannot find them and sets the hillside alight. Fire runs up through the trees. The two brothers climb above the smoke and run out of mountain. Balarama looks down. Krishna is a figure in the smoke with his back to the fire. For the first time in the film, they are afraid.

t: The leap and the false victory
sum: They leap from the burning peak and disappear. Jarasandha believes them dead and goes home to Magadha, satisfied.
why: A false victory for the antagonist; the audience knows he is wrong.
turn: He sees no bodies and accepts it.
story: They jump. The shot follows one silhouette against the flames and stops before the ground. The fire rises. At the bottom, Jarasandha waits for bodies. He sees none. A commander tells him there is no sign of them in the ash. He decides he has won, and goes home. On the hill, the fire burns out.

sum: Rukmī speaks of Jarasandha to his father and a visitor: the king who cannot be beaten, the army that rolls on. Rukmini, hearing from another room, understands the politics behind the match with Śiśupāla.
why: Gives Rukmini the political side of the same tale: the kings’ pride in Jarasandha against her wonder at Krishna’s patience.
turn: Rukmini understands her father will give way.
story: In the next room, Rukmī is telling his father how big Jarasandha’s army is. He says it as if he were describing his own. The father listens. Rukmini, behind a screen, hears what he is not saying: that the match with Śiśupāla is a way of being on the right side of that army. She understands that her father will give way.

sum: A soldier home from the north sits with a merchant and Rukmini, who stops to buy flowers. He says: seventeen times they beat him and let him go. She asks why. He cannot say.
why: Delivers Event 03 as a mystery: the strange patience of the unseen man.
turn: The soldier says “I do not know” and she smiles.
story: In the Kuṇḍina market, a soldier back from the north is telling a merchant about the war. Seventeen times, he says, they beat him and let him go. Rukmini is buying flowers. She stops. “Why?” she asks. He cannot say. “I do not know,” he says. She smiles. The soldier does not know what he said that was funny.

sum: As the next round with Jarasandha approaches, a stranger army arrives: Kālayavana, with thirty million barbarian troops. Banners the water-carrier has never seen cover the plain.
why: Raises the threat beyond the familiar; the two-front problem in one image.
turn: The new banner appears on the horizon.
story: The water-carrier is standing at the wall with a bucket when the horizon changes. The banners are not Jarasandha’s. They are a different colour and a different shape, and there are far more of them. Thirty million, someone says on the wall, and no one believes it until the plain is full. The carrier looks at his chalk marks. Then he looks at the new army, and puts the chalk away.

sum: Krishna and Balarama see danger from two sides: if Jarasandha comes while they fight Kālayavana, the people will be crushed between them. No option is safe.
why: A council in which every choice costs someone; sets the cause for Dvārakā.
turn: A map on the table shows the sea.
story: The council meets again. There are two enemies and one city. If Jarasandha comes while they fight the Yavana, the people are caught between them. Krishna’s voice goes through the options. One by one, each is shown to fail. Balarama hits the table. A map on the table shows the coast, a small shape on the edge of it, and the sea. The voice stops there.

sum: They decide to build a fortress no enemy can enter, settle the family there, and then deal with Kālayavana. Krishna stands at the shore.
why: The turn from defence to creation.
turn: He points to the water.
story: Krishna goes down to the shore at Ānarta. He stands at the edge of the water with his back to the camera. The wind moves his garment. He looks at the sea for a long time and then raises one hand, and points. The camera goes where the hand points: the sea, flat and empty.

t: The city rises from the sea
sum: A fortress twelve yojanas around rises from the ocean: gold gateways touching the sky, crystal terraces, jewelled houses, treasuries, stables, watchtowers, temples. Viśvakarmā’s craft shows in every line.
why: The film’s great spectacle of wonder; the city that becomes the ending’s place.
turn: The first gate rises from the water.
story: The first gate rises from the water. Then a wall, then towers, then terraces of crystal and gold. The sea parts and settles around them. Treasuries, stables, watchtowers and temples come up as if they had always been there. The Yādava sailors on the shore stop what they are doing. A woman puts her hand to her mouth. It takes less than a minute, and no one saw anyone build it.

sum: Indra gives the Sudharmā hall and the Pārijāta tree; Varuṇa gives swift horses; Kubera his eight treasures. The wealth of the world comes to the sea and none of it is asked for.
why: The world’s wealth returns to the one who does not seek it; the Pārijāta links back to the Manthana.
turn: The tree takes root in the courtyard.
story: The gods come to the new quay with gifts. Indra gives a great assembly hall and a tree in flower. Varuṇa leads out swift horses. Kubera sets down eight treasures and does not look at them. The tree takes root in the central court and its flowers open. They bow, in turn, to an empty seat. No one has asked for any of it.

t: The great move: waking in Dvārakā
sum: By yogic power all of Mathurā’s people are carried to Dvārakā in one move. They sleep in Mathurā and wake by the sea: children, cattle, carts, lamps.
why: A mass-evacuation set-piece with no enemy; wonder and displacement at once.
turn: A child laughs at the waves.
story: The city of Mathurā sleeps. In its streets lamps burn low. Somewhere a baby cries and is hushed. A light moves across the roofs, and everything is gone. In Dvārakā at dawn, the people wake in the same beds and carts and arms, and the sound they hear is the sea. A child runs to the edge of the street and laughs at the waves.

t: The lone walk from the gate
pl: The gate of Dvārakā; the road
sum: Krishna, unarmed and wearing a lotus garland, walks out through the city gate while the people sleep in safety. A guard watches him go.
why: The one man who goes out alone to absorb the threat; the image Rukmini carries of him.
turn: The gate closes behind him.
story: The city is asleep, and one man is not. He comes to the gate in a garland of lotuses. He carries no weapon. The guard sees him and does not know what to say. The man nods and goes out. A footprint is left in the dust. The gate closes. The guard stands there a long time.

t: The potter’s wheel by the waves
sum: A potter whose wheel was moved to the new quay sets it by the waves and turns the first pot of the new city.
why: World-welfare proof for Event 04: a people saved from a two-front war are settled.
turn: The first pot is lifted.
story: The potter’s wheel has been moved to the quay. He puts it where the wind comes off the water and spins it with his foot. He wets his hands, puts a ball of clay on the wheel and pulls. The first pot of the new city rises under his hands, rough and uneven. He sets it in the sun and the spray. A passer-by looks and walks on.

t: The sailors’ tale at the ferry
sum: A ferryman and two sailors from the coast argue about the city in the sea. One swears he has seen it; one says it is a story. Rukmini, crossing to visit a relative, listens from the back of the boat.
why: Delivers Event 04 as a travellers’ quarrel; gives her an image of a place she has never seen.
turn: One sailor describes the lamps lit all night.
story: A ferry crosses the river near Kuṇḍina. Two sailors from the coast are arguing with the ferryman about a city in the sea. One has seen it, he says. The other says it is a story. The ferryman rows and listens. Rukmini sits at the back of the boat with a basket. One of the sailors describes the lamps that are lit all night along the wall. She does not say anything, but her eyes follow the water.

sum: Rukmini has never seen the sea. A painted cloth or a sailor’s sketch shows the city. She traces the walls with her finger, then closes her eyes. The film shows what she imagines: a place as she needs it to be, not as it is.
why: Gives the ending its comparison: what she imagined against what she finds (E07-02).
turn: She makes her own picture.
story: At night in her room, Rukmini unrolls a painted cloth a sailor left behind. It shows a city on the sea. She traces the walls with her finger, then closes her eyes. The film shows what she sees: a place that is half the cloth and half her wish. The sea in it is bigger than any sea. The lamps are warmer. She opens her eyes, and the room is small.

sum: Nārada, the mischievous messenger, tells Kālayavana how to know Vāsudeva by his marks: the garland, the mark on the chest, the dark skin. He leaves, smiling.
why: A precise third-party description by an unreliable messenger; gives the audience a chart of marks without a face.
turn: Kālayavana repeats the marks aloud.
story: Nārada walks into Kālayavana’s camp as if he had been invited. He sits down and smiles. He says there is a man Kālayavana should know how to find, and he lists the marks: a garland of lotuses, a curl of hair on the chest, a certain dark colour of skin. He leaves before Kālayavana can ask who sent him. The Yavana repeats the list aloud to himself, as if learning a spell.

t: Kālayavana sees the man on foot
sum: A man walks out of the city, unarmed, wearing a lotus garland. Kālayavana sees the marks Nārada described and recognises him. He dismounts and decides to fight without weapons.
why: The recognition that starts the chase.
turn: He drops his weapon.
story: A man comes out of the gate of Mathurā alone, unarmed, wearing a garland of lotuses. Kālayavana, on the plain, sees him and straightens. He checks the marks against what he was told, one by one. They match. He gets off his horse, takes off his sword and lets it fall. He means to fight with his hands.

pl: Across the land to the mountains
sum: Krishna keeps just ahead of Kālayavana, always one step short, across fields and rivers to a mountain cave. Kālayavana taunts him as a coward. Krishna lets it be said.
why: A chase where the hunted is the hunter; patience as action; accepted shame to save others.
turn: The hills close in.
story: Kālayavana runs and does not catch him. The man ahead is always one step out of reach. They cross a field, a river and a ridge. Kālayavana shouts at him: coward, runaway, one who will not fight. The man does not turn. Behind them the army falls away and the country gets wilder. The hills close in. Ahead, there is a dark opening in the rock.

sum: Krishna enters a cave. Kālayavana follows into the dark and finds a man asleep. Taking him for Krishna pretending to sleep, he approaches.
why: The trap: a room with a sleeper and an arrogant intruder.
turn: He raises his foot.
story: The cave is dark and goes back a long way. A slender figure slips in ahead of Kālayavana and is gone behind a rock. Kālayavana follows, breathing hard. At the far end, in a patch of dimness, a man lies asleep. His chest barely moves. Kālayavana, who has been chasing a trick, sees what he takes for another. He walks up to the sleeper and lifts his foot.

sum: Kālayavana kicks the sleeper. Mucukunda wakes, angry, and looks at him. Kālayavana burns to ash.
why: A short, silent, frightening fight with no weapon; an act of arrogance wakes something that burns.
turn: The sleeper’s eyes open.
story: The foot lands. Mucukunda’s eyes open. He is angry and he looks at what has woken him. For half a second there is nothing. Then the light from his eyes fills the cave. When it clears there is only a shape of ash on the floor. Mucukunda sits up slowly. Behind a rock, someone waits.

sum: Mucukunda, a king of the Ikṣvāku line, fought for the Devas against the Asuras. Offered a boon, he asked for undisturbed sleep, with the power to burn whoever woke him. When Kārttikeya became general, he was released from service and chose sleep over liberation.
why: Links Event 05 to the Manthana; the cave as a place where ages sleep.
turn: He closes his eyes.
story: Long ago, Mucukunda fought for the gods against the demons, and fought well. The war went on for ages. At the end he was offered a gift, and he asked for sleep. Let no one wake me, he said, and let whoever does be burnt. He found a cave and lay down. When the gods gave him leave to be free he chose to sleep on. The scene is told in three images: a battle, a bargain and a closing of eyes.

sum: A figure steps into the light. Mucukunda, a king who has slept through ages, sees a man of unearthly radiance and wonders if this is the Supreme Lord. His face is the whole scene.
why: The film’s purest portrait of Krishna by an awed face; the illumination method at its smallest scale.
turn: He bows.
story: A figure steps into the light. Mucukunda sits on the cave floor and looks up. He does not know him, and he does. A light falls on his face from somewhere to the left, and the camera stays on him as his expression changes: surprise, doubt, recognition, and something like grief. His lips move. He bows his head. A tear runs down the old face. The film has promised the audience a portrait of Krishna, and this is it.

sum: Mucukunda asks who he is. A voice says: my births are countless; in this age I came as Vasudeva’s son to protect dharma; I killed Kaṁsa; your glance burned Kālayavana; I came because you once prayed for me.
why: His account of himself, heard by someone who believes it; the closest to a statement of identity the film allows.
turn: He recalls Garga’s prediction.
story: Mucukunda asks who he is. A voice answers from the light. My births are countless, it says. In this age I came as Vasudeva’s son to protect dharma. I killed Kaṁsa. Your glance burned the Yavana, and I came because you once prayed for me. Mucukunda’s face changes as each line lands. He remembers an old sage, Garga, and what he said about this day.

sum: Mucukunda prays: the delusion of worldly happiness, the rarity of human birth, the waste of kingship, death like a snake, the futility of power, freedom through good company. He asks only to serve.
why: The most intimate portrait of the Lord in the whole gathering; the awed witness speaks.
turn: He asks for nothing.
story: Mucukunda’s prayer is long, and the film lets it be. He says that worldly happiness is a dream, that a human birth is rare, that he spent his on a kingdom and did not know it. He says power is a thing that ends, and death comes like a snake. He asks for only one thing: to be close to those who know the Lord. The camera stays on his face and the light on it does not move.

sum: Krishna offers boons. Mucukunda declines every one. Krishna praises his steadiness and says the offer was a test.
why: A man who gives up wealth for the sake of the truth he saw; a light for Rukmini’s plea.
turn: He says “nothing”.
story: The Lord offers him anything. Mucukunda thinks, and says nothing. He is offered it again. He shakes his head. He asks for nothing at all. The voice says something that sounds like laughter. It was a test, it says, and he has passed it. Mucukunda does not seem to care. He bows.

sum: Mucukunda leaves the cave, judges that the age has changed, and walks north to Badarikāśrama to worship Hari.
why: A man leaves the world he woke into; the witness departs.
turn: He looks back once.
story: Mucukunda comes out of the cave into daylight. He has not seen it for a very long time. He looks at the plants, the sky, the people. He sees that the world has changed and that the age has too. He turns north, and walks. At the top of a rise, he looks back once, then goes on.

sum: Krishna returns to Mathurā, destroys the barbarian army and sends its wealth toward Dvārakā.
why: A summary beat: the second siege ends.
turn: The gate opens.
story: The gate of Mathurā opens. Outside, the plain is full of the Yavana army and, in the next shot, nearly empty. There is wreckage and silence. Carts are loaded with the dead army’s wealth and set on the road toward the sea. The water-carrier on the wall looks at his chalk marks and chalks a line under the last of them.

sum: A goatherd whose flock grazes near the mountain sees smoke from the cave and, later, a sage passing. When the siege is lifted, the goats walk back onto the road.
why: World-welfare proof for Event 05.
turn: The goats walk onto the road.
story: A goatherd and his flock graze on a mountain slope. He sees smoke from the cave and moves the goats away. Later he sees an old man pass, walking north. When the news comes that the siege is lifted, he leads the goats down to the road, and they walk onto it as if nothing had been wrong.

sum: A herdsman tells a friend: a Yavana ran in after a man, and only smoke came out. Rukmini, filling a jar, hears. She asks which man. He does not know. She remembers the garland and the lone walk (E04-07).
why: Delivers Event 05 as a rumour; gives Rukmini her private picture of him: the man who walks out alone.
turn: She asks if he had a garland.
story: At a well near Kuṇḍina, a herdsman says to a friend: a Yavana ran into a cave after a man, and only smoke came out. Rukmini, filling her jar, stops. “What man?” He does not know. “Did he wear a garland?” He says it is possible. Rukmini turns to go, and the jar is lighter than it should be.

sum: A priest recites Mucukunda’s prayer to Rukmini’s mother and Rukmini: the king who gave up kingship after seeing him. Rukmini, hearing, is silent for a long moment.
why: Delivers Event 05’s most intimate account of Krishna by someone who truly saw him.
turn: She asks the priest to say it again.
story: In the temple of Ambikā, a priest recites to Rukmini’s mother and to Rukmini. He tells of a king who slept for ages, who woke, and who asked for nothing. The prayer is in his voice, slow and precise. Rukmini says nothing for a long moment. Then she asks the priest to say it again.

sum: A visitor, trading gossip, lists the marks by which Vāsudeva is known, as Nārada gave them to Kālayavana. Rukmini’s maid giggles; Rukmini checks each against what she has heard.
why: The closest the film comes to an exact description by a third party; it is also the audience’s checklist for E06-18.
turn: She asks about a mark and the visitor cannot answer.
story: A visitor to the palace is trading gossip about Krishna. He tells the marks as he heard them. The maid giggles at one. Rukmini, calmly and almost to herself, checks each against what she has heard: this one is right, that one is not. The visitor stops, a little offended. Rukmini smiles. There is a detail he got wrong, and she knows it.

t: The question that frames the telling
pl: The court of Parīkṣit; or a bard’s fire
sum: Parīkṣit asks Śuka how Krishna won Rukmiṇī, having heard it was a rākṣasa-style marriage. Śuka begins. In the film’s version a bard answers a listener’s question: “They say he stole her.”
why: A frame that lets the film answer the objection (“abduction”) with Rukmini’s choice.
turn: The bard says: “She wrote the letter.”
story: A fire at night and a small group around it. A listener asks the bard the thing he has heard: that Krishna stole a king’s daughter. The bard looks into the fire. “That is what they say,” he says. “They do not say that she wrote to him first.” The listener opens his mouth to ask, and the bard starts the story. The fire fades into a morning in Kuṇḍina.

sum: Visitors sing of Krishna’s qualities, beauty and valour. Rukmini, listening at the edge of the hall, decides he is the right husband. Elsewhere he judges her the right wife.
why: The first and most important source of her image of him; the film’s inciting wish.
turn: She decides.
story: Visitors sing in her father’s hall. The first sings of his valour, the second of the gods he has met, the third of his beauty. Rukmini listens from the gallery with a hand on the rail. They disagree about his face, but the same man runs through all three songs. When the last singer stops, she realises she has made up her mind. She does not move. In another city, someone has made up his.

sum: Rukmī, hostile to Krishna, blocks the family’s inclination and arranges the match with Śiśupāla. Bhīṣmaka, who is inclined to Krishna, yields out of love for his son. Rukmini is overridden.
why: The inciting incident: her choice is cancelled by the person who should protect her.
turn: Her father gives way.
story: Rukmī brings the news of the match in front of the whole household. He has settled it with Śiśupāla’s father. Rukmini says she has other wishes. Rukmī says what he thinks of the cowherd she means. She looks at her father. Bhīṣmaka looks down. He loves his son, and she sees it. Rukmī goes on talking. She does not cry. The scene ends on her silence.

sum: Distressed, Rukmini sends a trusted brāhmaṇa to Krishna. She writes the letter: I have chosen you; no sensible maiden would choose another; if you do not come I will give up my life; come in secret; the plan is the temple procession. She seals it and gives it to him.
why: Her first act and the film’s first turning point: an irreversible, active choice that carries the plan.
turn: She seals it and gives it away.
story: She sits down at night and takes out the ink. She has been taught how to write letters to kings. She writes to one. Every sentence costs her. She says she has chosen him. She says no sensible girl would choose another. She names the day and describes how it may be done. She says that if he does not come she will give up her life and try again in the next. She seals it, sends for the Brahmin and puts it in his hands.

pl: The road from Kuṇḍina to Dvārakā
sum: The Brahmin carries the letter on a long road: a guard post, a river crossing, a pursuer sent by Rukmī. Each is a small test; he thinks the letter is heavier than gold.
why: Action with a plain man as the hero; the carrier as protagonist of the middle.
turn: He crosses the river with the letter dry.
story: The Brahmin leaves before dawn with the letter in his clothes. At a guard post, a soldier asks his business, and the Brahmin says something about a pilgrimage. A river is up and the ferryman refuses to cross until the Brahmin pays him double. A rider appears on the road behind him. He walks faster, then slower, and the rider goes by. The Brahmin takes the letter out at the next village and checks that it is dry.

sum: The Brahmin is received, honoured and fed. Krishna massages his feet and asks about his welfare, his duties, his king, and offers help. The Brahmin tells him everything and reads the letter. He asks Krishna to decide promptly.
why: The honest portrait of a man who massages a messenger’s feet; the only eyewitness account before the temple.
turn: Krishna reads the letter and smiles.
story: The Brahmin is brought into a hall and sits down. Someone washes his feet, and it is not a servant. Hands: warm, careful. A voice asks about his journey, about his duties, whether his king protects his people, and whether he needs anything. The Brahmin, who has been rehearsing a speech for days, forgets it. He takes out the letter and reads it aloud. When he finishes, he asks the Lord to decide quickly.

pl: The road from Ānarta to Vidarbha, one night
sum: Krishna hears the wedding time, orders his chariot; Dāruka brings it. He and the Brahmin ride from Ānarta to Vidarbha in a single night: dark road, hooves, dawn light.
why: Suspense without sight; the unseen man is on his way.
turn: Dawn breaks on the plain of Vidarbha.
story: He reads the time of the wedding, calls for the chariot and does not wait to be asked twice. Dāruka brings it. The Brahmin climbs in. They leave in the dark. The road goes under the wheels, the stars turn over, and the horses do not slow. Somewhere in the night the Brahmin closes his eyes. When he opens them there is a grey line in the east, and the plain of Vidarbha.

sum: Bhīṣmaka prepares for Śiśupāla’s wedding. The city is cleaned and decorated, rituals performed, gifts given. Rukmini is bathed and adorned: ritual as imprisonment.
why: Suffocation: she is dressed for a wedding she does not want.
turn: She hides something in a fold of the dress.
story: The city is cleaned and hung with flowers. Priests chant. Gifts are given. In the women’s quarters Rukmini is bathed, dressed and adorned until she can barely move. Bangles close on her wrists. Each ornament is a fastening. A maid holds up a mirror. She looks at the stranger in it, and slips something into a fold of the dress.

sum: Damaghoṣa arrives with an army; Jarasandha, Śālva, Dantavakra, Vidūratha, Pauṇḍraka and thousands of kings come as Śiśupāla’s allies and vow to fight Krishna if he steals the bride.
why: A city on the edge of a massacre; the coalition of kings made visible; the Earth’s burden at Kuṇḍina.
turn: The vow is sworn aloud.
story: The kings arrive in a long column. Damaghoṣa comes with an army, then Jarasandha, then Śālva, Dantavakra, Vidūratha and Pauṇḍraka, each with an escort. In the hall they give the vow together, and then separately: if Krishna comes to steal her, we will fight him. Rukmini hears about it from a window. She counts the banners. There are too many to count.

sum: Balarama, fearing conflict and out of love for his brother, hurries to Kuṇḍina with a large army.
why: A brother’s love sends an army before he is asked.
turn: He gives the order to march.
story: Balarama is not asked. He hears the kings are gathering and that his brother has gone alone, and he gathers an army. He leaves at once with a large force. On the road he is silent. A captain asks if there is trouble. He says there will be. The army marches on through the afternoon.

sum: The hour is near. Krishna and the Brahmin have not come. She imagines reasons, including the displeasure of Brahmā or Śiva, and consoles herself that the time has not yet passed.
why: The low point: hope turning to dread.
turn: She prays to the very gods she fears.
story: The hour is near, and the Brahmin has not returned. Rukmini sits in her room dressed for the wedding and waits. She imagines that he never arrived, that the letter was refused, that the gods are angry with her, that she asked too much. She goes through every reason in order. The lamp burns lower. A maid brings food and takes it away again. She starts to pray to the gods she is afraid of.

sum: Her left eye, arm and thigh twitch: a good sign. The Brahmin walks in smiling, joyful, with Krishna’s message and promise.
why: Dread breaks; the answer to her letter arrives as a report.
turn: He walks in smiling before he speaks.
story: Her left eye twitches, then her arm, then her thigh. She is not sure whether to trust it. A moment later the door opens and the Brahmin comes in, smiling. He does not say anything for a moment, and it is enough. Then he cannot stop. He tells her what he saw: the city in the sea, the gold gates, the lamps. He tells her that the man himself washed his feet. He says the man told him he could not sleep either. Rukmini laughs, and then cries.

sum: Rukmini bows to the Brahmin. Bhīṣmaka receives Krishna and Balarama with honour and hosts the other kings by rank.
why: The father’s quiet sorrow and hospitality; the family’s divided loyalty.
turn: He greets Krishna.
story: At the gate of the palace Bhīṣmaka waits for two arrivals. He has sent his steward ahead, and he goes down himself. His face tells the story: he is relieved, afraid and grateful at once. The guests arrive; the camera is on him. He bows. He leads them in by the right hand, and the crowd closes behind. He knows what he has done, and what it will cost him.

sum: The citizens gaze at Krishna and wish Rukmini may marry him, offering their merit.
why: A whole city offers its merit for a bride’s choice; public hope she can hear.
turn: A woman lifts a garland toward her window.
story: In the street below her window the citizens are looking at someone she cannot see. They talk quietly. A woman holds up a garland. An old man says he would give his merit if she could marry him. A child says the same thing, a little louder. The street takes it up in murmurs. Rukmini, behind the screen, hears it all, and does not look.

pl: The road from the palace to Ambikā’s temple
sum: Rukmini leaves the palace for the Ambikā temple, guarded and accompanied by her mothers, friends, musicians and bards amid drums, conches and horns. A ring of soldiers surrounds her.
why: Escape through ceremony: the plan begins as a pageant.
turn: She steps over the temple threshold.
story: She leaves the palace for the temple with a ring of soldiers around her. Her mothers walk ahead, her friends behind. Musicians play, conches sound, bards sing the old stories under their breath, and one of them, softly, sings the one about the goddess who passed every claimant. The soldiers watch the road for any sign of him. She looks straight ahead. The temple door is at the end.

sum: She washes, enters, is guided by brāhmaṇa women in worship, prays that Krishna become her husband, and receives blessings and prasāda. The temple wall behind her holds the panels of the Churning.
why: A silent request at the shrine of the goddess who held Śiva’s poison; she asks for nothing but him.
turn: She lifts her eyes from the idol.
story: She washes, enters, and kneels in front of the goddess. The temple women guide her through the worship. She asks for what she came to ask. She does not ask to be saved. She asks to be able to bear whatever she has chosen. The goddess’s eyes are painted, and her hands are open. Behind her on the wall is the panel with the poison and the throat. She takes the blessings and the food and stands.

pl: The temple door and the forecourt
sum: She breaks her vow of silence and walks out, led by a maidservant, among the assembled kings, who are stunned by her.
why: Her voice, her public act; the first step of the climax.
turn: She speaks.
story: She comes out of the temple door with her friends behind her. A maid takes her hand. She breaks her vow of silence and says something no one hears. Then she walks, slowly, into the forecourt, among the kings. They have been waiting for the bride to pass. They stop talking. One of them drops a cup. She walks past them as if they were furniture.

sum: She advances shyly, glancing at the kings. She sees Krishna and is eager to mount his chariot.
why: Recognition at last; the moment the whole film delays; reversal and recognition in one beat.
turn: Her eyes find him.
story: She walks across the stones with her eyes down. Then she lifts them, and sees him. The camera is hers. He is standing in a chariot at the edge of the forecourt. He is not any of the songs, and all of them. She sees why the singers could not agree: each had caught him in a different light. Now there is only this one. The blue light, withheld all film, arrives. No one says his name.

sum: He seizes her before his enemies and lifts her onto the chariot. She has chosen it: she goes willingly.
why: Seizing and choosing at once: she chooses to be taken. The film’s theme in an act.
turn: Her foot leaves the ground.
story: He does not wait for her to climb. He takes her in his arms in front of every king and sets her beside him. The chariot jolts. Her foot is already on the board. Dāruka’s hands are on the reins. For half a second no one understands what has happened. She turns and looks at the faces behind her, and does not look back at the temple.

sum: He drives off through the ring of kings with Balarama leading, like a lion taking its prey from jackals. The conch sounds.
why: Release of energy after the lift; the kings’ humiliation made visible.
turn: The ring breaks.
story: The chariot goes through the ring of kings like a lion through jackals. Balarama’s men open the way in front. The conch sounds, long and clear. The kings draw swords too late. Rukmini holds the rail and does not look down. The road opens in front of them. Behind her, a hundred horses turn at once.

sum: Jarasandha and the others cannot bear it. They lament that “mere cowherds” took their honour. Śiśupāla stands in the groom’s clothes.
why: The kings’ humiliation; a rare scene from the losers’ side.
turn: Śiśupāla looks at his empty hands.
story: The kings stand where the chariot was. Jarasandha says they have been robbed by cowherds. Dantavakra swears. Śālva looks at his own hands. In the middle of them stands Śiśupāla in his groom’s clothes with the garland still on his neck. He looks at the empty ground where the bride walked. No one says anything to him.

t: The pursuit and the Yadava defence
sum: The enraged kings arm and chase. The Yadava commanders turn to face them. Arrows fall; Rukmini fears for her husband’s army. Krishna’s voice reassures her: your side will soon destroy them. Gada, Saṅkarṣaṇa and others strike down horses, elephants and chariots.
why: The first test of her choice: she fears for the people who came for her.
turn: The Yadava line holds.
story: The kings arm and chase. Behind the chariot the Yādava commanders turn and face them. Arrows fall like rain. Rukmini sees them land and thinks, for the first time, of the men who are dying for her. Beside her, a voice says, quietly, that her side will soon destroy them. She looks. Behind them, horses go down, elephants turn, and the chase breaks into pieces.

sum: Jarasandha sees his side destroyed and withdraws. He consoles the dejected Śiśupāla: victory and defeat are governed by time and fate; the kings will prevail when time turns. They go home.
why: Philosophy as a way of saving face; the coalition’s habit of consoling itself.
turn: Śiśupāla accepts the consolation.
story: The kings come off the field in pieces. Jarasandha finds Śiśupāla standing with his hands empty. He talks to him as to a son. Victory and defeat, he says, belong to time and fate. Time turns, and when it does, we will win. Śiśupāla listens and nods. The kings go home. The camera stays on the road a moment after they have gone.

sum: Rukmī, unable to bear it, pursues with a division and vows before the kings not to re-enter Kuṇḍina until he has killed Krishna and recovered his sister.
why: A public vow that locks him out of his own home; the personal opponent’s peak.
turn: He swears.
story: Rukmī cannot bear it. He turns on his horse in front of the kings and swears that he will not enter Kuṇḍina again until he has killed the cowherd and brought his sister back. The kings watch. He gathers one division and goes after the chariot alone. Behind him, nobody tries to stop him.

sum: Rukmī attacks. Krishna breaks each of his bows, destroys his weapons and shield. Rukmī leaps down with a sword; Krishna cuts it to pieces and readies his own to kill him. Rukmini watches the two men she loves try to kill each other.
why: Brother against husband; the longest scene where Krishna acts.
turn: The sword is raised.
story: Rukmī catches up. He attacks, and Krishna breaks his bow. He takes another, and it breaks. He takes a third. Weapon after weapon, shield after shield, until Rukmī leaps down with a sword in his hand. Krishna cuts it to pieces. He turns his own sword. Rukmini, in the chariot, watches the two men she loves move toward the end.

sum: Rukmini falls at Krishna’s feet and begs for her brother’s life. He stops.
why: Her second decisive act: on her knees at the feet of the man who has just saved her. Mercy won.
turn: He lowers the sword.
story: She goes to her knees. Nothing in her had planned it. She puts her arms around his feet and asks for her brother’s life. The sword is above her. The world is still. She does not look up. Then the blade comes down, empty, and her husband lowers it. Rukmini’s head is still bowed. She does not move for a long time.

sum: Krishna binds Rukmī with cloth and shaves part of his hair and moustache. Mercy and humiliation in the same stroke. Rukmini looks away.
why: The cost of mercy: the brother lives but is shamed.
turn: The razor.
story: He binds Rukmī with a strip of cloth and cuts away half his moustache and half his hair. It is mercy and it is humiliation, in one gesture. Rukmī does not struggle. Rukmini looks away. The cut hair falls on the road. The wind takes some of it.

sum: Balarama frees Rukmī and rebukes Krishna: this is not worthy of our family.
why: Two brothers in moral disagreement in front of the bride; Balarama’s two loyalties.
turn: Krishna does not answer.
story: Balarama arrives with his army and sees what has been done. He frees Rukmī and turns to his brother. This is not worthy of us, he says. It was not a matter for shame. Krishna does not answer. Rukmini stands between them and says nothing. The wind moves the cut hair along the road.

sum: Balarama consoles Rukmini: people bear their own joy and sorrow; the self is not the body; a warrior’s duties can be harsh. She calms.
why: A brother-in-law becomes a teacher in a moment of grief; the first time someone close to Krishna speaks of him as a person.
turn: She wipes her face.
story: Balarama sits down beside Rukmini on the ground. He tells her that each person bears their own joy and their own sorrow. He tells her that the self is not the body. He says a warrior’s duties can be harsh, and that her brother has met his. He does not tell her it will not hurt. She listens, wipes her face with the end of her veil, and nods.

sum: Humiliated, Rukmī builds the city of Bhojakaṭa and will not return to Kuṇḍina.
why: A proud man builds a city so he need not go home; the cost.
turn: The first wall rises.
story: Rukmī does not go home. He has sworn, and he keeps his word. On a river plain far from Kuṇḍina he sets a stake in the ground and has a wall built round it. The first walls go up. Workers lay stone. A city is made of an oath. He stands on the rampart in the evening and looks toward home.

sum: The flower vendor’s garlands are used for a different bride. The weaver’s wedding cloth is carried away on a chariot. The ferryman takes a Yadava soldier across the river and no one else.
why: World-welfare proof for Event 06: a coerced alliance does not bind two kingdoms to war; markets return.
turn: A bride at another house wears the vendor’s garlands.
story: The wedding is off and the flower vendor finds her garlands used for another bride at another door. The weaver’s wedding cloth, woven for a day that did not come, rides out on the back of a chariot. The ferryman takes one Yādava soldier across the river and refuses everyone else. Three small stories in a single morning. None of them know who took the bride. All of them are glad.

t: The cut: from the road to the city
sum: The text says Krishna marries her according to Vedic rites and takes her to Dvārakā. The film shows none of it. A cut goes from the road, after Balarama’s consolation, to the city, with the ceremony left as a gap.
why: Keeps the project rule: no marriage on screen, nothing after.
turn: The sea appears at the edge of the road.
story: The road. Balarama’s consolation is over, and the chariot goes on. The text says that rites were done, and the film shows none of them. A cut: the wheels, the dust, a gap in the hills, and a line of light where the land ends. Somewhere in that gap a marriage has happened, and we are not shown it. The sea comes into view at the edge of the road.

sum: Rukmini, who has lived inland, sees the ocean for the first time from the chariot, with a city rising from the water. She compares it with what she imagined.
why: A second first sight: the sea, answering the stories; the first reversal of expectation.
turn: She sees the gold gate.
story: She has never seen the sea. From the chariot it comes first as a line, then as a wideness that does not end, then as a gold gate standing in the water. It is not the city of the songs. It is more, and it is smaller. She holds the rail. The wind pulls at her veil. She does not say anything. She is aware that he is beside her, and that the sea has her whole attention.

sum: Dvārakā is decorated; guests from many clans rejoice; citizens offer jewelled gifts; doorways have lamps; flowers on the streets. The vendor, water-carrier, potter, goatherd, farmer and fisher family appear, each in a doorway. A cow lies down in the street. The wall is clean.
why: The ledger closes: the world’s gains seen at once.
turn: The water-carrier raises a hand beside a clean wall.
story: The city has come out into the street. Doors are hung with lamps. Flowers lie on the ground. The vendor from Kuṇḍina stands at a corner with her basket, the water-carrier beside a clean wall, the potter at his wheel, the goatherd with his goats, the farmer with his cow, and the fisher family on the quay. Each lifts a hand. Citizens give gifts. The chariot goes through them slowly. In one wide shot, every one of them is in a doorway.

sum: Her lamp from Kuṇḍina, carried in her hands; a matching lamp already lit in Dvārakā. She sets hers beside it.
why: The answer to the letter; the twin-lamps motif.
turn: She sees the second lamp already lit.
story: In her new room she takes the lamp she carried from Kuṇḍina out of her bag. She has kept it through all of it. She puts it down on a ledge and sees that another lamp is already burning there, the same shape. A hand has lit it. She stands a long time. She lights her own and sets it beside the first.

sum: In the middle of the joy, a place is laid for a brother who will not come. A thread to Bhojakaṭa.
why: The cost of the day: Rukmī’s absence.
turn: She notices the empty place.
story: In the middle of the feast a place is laid for someone. A small cup, a plate, a space at the end of the table. Nobody sits there. The talk goes on. Rukmini sees the place and then looks at the door. She does not say anything. Beside her, someone sees her look, and sets the place a little straighter. The meal goes on.

sum: A bard sings the story of the abduction, as the text says it was sung through the land. It is her side of the story. The kings hear it.
why: The story becomes the song; the bard closes his frame.
turn: The bard includes her letter.
story: In a courtyard a bard begins to sing. It is the story of a girl in Vidarbha who heard of a man, and wrote to him, and walked out of a temple. He sings it from her side, which no one has ever done. Among the listeners are kings who came to the wedding as friends of the other side. They listen. At the end, the bard looks across the courtyard. She is there, and he bows.

t: What he says, and does not say
sum: A line or a silence: his reply to her letter, or her telling him what she saw at the temple (the reverse of the letter). One of the two speaks.
why: The film’s last exchange; she lights him now.
turn: One of them speaks.
story: On a terrace by the sea, the two of them. One of them has to speak. If it is he, he answers her letter. If it is she, she tells him what she saw at the temple. The evening is almost over. A line, or a silence, and the film chooses one. The sea is loud behind them. She looks at him for the first time as a man and not a story.

t: Together at the edge of the sea
sum: The two stand side by side, in profile or from behind, with Rukmini the visual centre. The image is held a little longer than any shot of Krishna in the film.
why: The last image: two people in one frame after a film in which one has barely been seen.
turn: The held shot.
story: The two of them stand side by side at the edge of the sea, in profile or from behind. The light is long and low. Rukmini is the centre of the frame. She does not look at him. For the first time in the film there is no one else in the frame. The shot is held a little longer than any shot of him has been held. Then the film ends.

sum: An infant is born with three eyes and four arms. A heavenly voice says the marks will vanish when the child is placed on the lap of the one who will cause his death.
why: Gives the rival’s life a prophecy; the invisible countdown.
turn: The voice speaks.
story: A child is born in the palace of Chedi, and the room goes quiet. He has three eyes and four arms. The queen looks at him and the midwives step back. A voice from the sky speaks: the extra arms and the third eye will fall away when he is placed on the lap of the one who will cause his death. The king and queen listen. No one asks the voice who that will be.

sum: Krishna visits and takes the infant on his lap; the extra arms and eye vanish. The mother realises that the one who restored her child may also be the one destined to kill him.
why: Recognition tinged with horror; the first meeting of Krishna and Śiśupāla.
turn: The marks vanish.
story: Krishna comes to the palace on a visit. The mother puts the child on his lap, because she has been told to. The extra arms and the eye vanish. She holds her breath. The child is just a child. She understands, all at once, that the man who made her son whole is the man who will end him. The scene ends on her face, not on his.

sum: The mother begs Krishna to spare her son. Krishna promises to tolerate one hundred offences.
why: The film’s clock; a bargain made with the one who will take her son.
turn: Krishna agrees.
story: She asks him to spare her son. He is kind and says he will pardon his faults. She asks how many. He says a hundred. She nods, and does not tell her son. The camera is on her. The number goes into the film like a clock that starts ticking and cannot be heard.

sum: The four Kumāras visit Vaikuṇṭha and are stopped by the gatekeepers Jaya and Vijaya. They curse them to be born in the world. Viṣṇu gives them a choice: seven births as devotees or three births as enemies. They choose three.
why: A cosmic curse behind Śiśupāla’s life, mirroring Durvāsā’s curse.
turn: They choose three births as enemies.
story: At the gate of Vaikuṇṭha two guards stop four sages. The sages are children in appearance and ancient in fact. Jaya and Vijaya say no one may enter. The sages curse them to be born in the world below. The Lord himself comes to the gate, and the guards fall at his feet. They can have seven births as his friends, or three as his enemies. They choose three, because they cannot bear to be away from him longer.

sum: Śiśupāla, in his groom’s clothes, finds the bride gone. His hostility hardens.
why: The rival’s wound; his humiliation as a reason for later hatred.
turn: He realises she left willingly.
story: In groom’s clothes with a garland on his neck, Śiśupāla waits at the temple. He has been told a bride will come. The forecourt is empty. He turns to someone and asks. They tell him. He looks at the road, and then at his own hands. He understands that she went willingly. His face changes slowly, and what takes its place is not grief.

sum: A man who defends his brother with an army and rebukes him for the shaving. Two loyalties in one man.
why: Deepens Balarama’s role beyond E06-28; a possible second beat.
turn: He chooses justice for Rukmī.
story: Balarama has defended his brother with an army, and he is not silent. He tells him the shaving was not worthy. He says it again more quietly. Then he turns to the army and tells them to stand down. He keeps both loyalties and does not pretend they are one. The scene ends on his back as he walks away.

sum: Control, vow and ruin as a single arc: a brother who arranges a match, swears an oath, loses a duel and builds a city so he need not go home.
why: The personal opponent’s arc in one scene; a possible single-scene summary.
turn: He swears the oath.
story: Rukmī arranges a match. He swears an oath. He loses a duel. He builds a city. Four short images: a hall in which his voice is the loudest, a roadside where he swears, a road where he falls, a plain where he lays the first stone. The man does not change between them. The only thing that changes is how much he has left.
